ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all UBOs, general partners, limited partners with control rights, directors and authorized signatories against the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, Government of Canada Special Economic Measures Regulations, OFAC SDN List, EU consolidated financial sanctions list, and applicable provincial/domestic watchlists; mandatory politically exposed person (PEP) screening at onboarding and on an ongoing basis under the PCMLTFA and FINTRAC guidance; enhanced due diligence required for foreign and domestic PEPs, family members and close associates; adverse media and law enforcement database checks are expected; all records must be retained for at least five years following termination of the business relationship.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Quebec official online portal (Le Registre des entreprises / REQ, accessible at registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The name must be predominantly in French under the Charter of the French Language; an acceptable non-French only name must be paired with a French version or have a recognized form; for a limited partnership, the name must include the expression 'societe en commandite' or the abbreviation 'S.E.C.'; transliteration rules require French characters and a clear representation of the legal form; the name must be distinctive and not cause confusion with other existing enterprises registered in Quebec.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Quebec in a way that implies public affiliation without prior ministerial consent
Inc., Ltd., LLC, Corp., societe par actions, or any token suggesting a legal form other than limited partnership
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon refusal, the Registraire issues a written notice stating the grounds. The applicant may submit written representations to the Registraire within 30 days of the refusal, citing the legal basis for distinctiveness and compliance with naming regulations, and may request reconsideration before expiry of the original search results. If the Registraire confirms the refusal, the applicant may apply to the Tribunal administratif du Quebec for review in accordance with the Act respecting legal publicity of enterprises within the applicable procedural delays; further recourse lies to the Superior Court of Quebec by way of judicial review. Where the refusal is based solely on a prior conflicting name, fresh clearance may be filed under an amended distinguishing name.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for registry and service-of-process purposes in Quebec, but not as a substitute for real commercial substance. For a PropTech/software-as-a-service business, Revenu Quebec and financial institutions generally accept a virtual office only when paired with a physical management address, operational presence, bank account, and business records maintained in Quebec; a virtual-only address may increase audit and substance review risk.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low quantified risk: approximately 10% in the first 12 months under random administrative verification of registered offices; increases to approximately 20-25% over a three-year horizon where the registered office is a mass virtual-office address or where Revenu Quebec initiates a GST/QST or payroll compliance audit. No routine unannounced physical inspection is prescribed for a low-risk software entity, but inspectors may visit when documentary discrepancies or red flags are identified.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Civil Code of Québec, Book 4, Chapter 2, Division 2 (arts. 2236-2247) respecting Limited Partnerships; Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, CQLR c. P-44.1, arts. 21, 30, 36-38; Regulation respecting the fees prescribed in application of the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, CQLR c. P-44.1, r. 1.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (directorate of Revenu Québec), 2050 rue de Bleury, Montréal QC H3A 2J5; secured online filing via the Registraire's services portal.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Déclaration d'immatriculation (Declaration of Registration) — official form for the constitution and registration of a société en commandite (limited partnership) under the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital and no escrow or capital deposit requirement for a Québec limited partnership. Each limited partner must validly make the contribution agreed in the partnership agreement; a limited partner who has not contributed acquires status only upon actual contribution. The general partner has full capacity to bind the partnership and is unlimitedly liable for its obligations.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED: That the General Partner subscribe to a 1% general partnership interest and that the initial Limited Partners, as listed in the Limited Partnership Agreement, subscribe to the remaining 99% limited partnership interests; FURTHER RESOLVED: That the registered office of the Partnership be established at [address], Québec, and the Registraire des entreprises du Québec be recognized as the competent registry authority; FURTHER RESOLVED: That [Name] be appointed President and Chief Executive Officer and [Name] be appointed Secretary-Treasurer, each authorized to execute filings, pay fees, open bank accounts and conclude contracts in the ordinary course; All prior acts of the officers in the Partnership's name are hereby ratified.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name Search and NUANS Report Reservation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec — name search and reservation service (online)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the proposed name through the Registraire's online name search tool and request a NUANS report to verify distinctiveness and conformity with arts. 10-14 of the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises. Reserve the approved name for up to 120 days; the reservation may be renewed once if no declaration of registration has been filed.
required_dossiers: Completed online name request form
NUANS computer-assisted name search report
Sectoral authorization or professional opinion letter if the name suggests a regulated activity
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the proposed name is refused, the partnership may file a corrected request with a new distinctive element or apply to the director of the Registraire for review of the refusal within the delay prescribed by law.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Execution of the Limited Partnership Agreement and Capital Subscription
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Legal counsel and the partners (general and limited partners) — notarization recommended for asset contributions
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft and execute a written limited partnership agreement complying with CCQ arts. 2236-2247. Specify the general partner's unlimited liability, the limited partners' agreed contributions (money, property or services), restrictions on limited partner participation in management, allocation of profits and losses, transfer restrictions and dissolution terms. Record subscriptions on a capital account schedule. No escrow or deposit of capital with a third party is required by provincial law.
required_dossiers: Genearl partner's constating documents and resolution if it is a corporation
Initial list of limited partners with names, addresses and contribution amounts
Signed limited partnership agreement
Subscription schedule and capital account ledger
Consent to the registered office by the legal owner (lease or letter of consent)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Subsequent corrections shall be made by supplemental agreement executed by all partners; any defective capital contribution is cured by actual delivery of the promised contribution, failing which the limited partner may be excluded or lose limited liability status as provided in CCQ art. 2240.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing of the Declaration of Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec — online declarative service (services.registraireentreprises.gouv.qc.ca)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Access the secured portal, select the declaration of registration for a limited partnership, and complete all required particulars: proposed or reserved name, head office address in Québec, domicile and name of each general partner, authorized persons, purposes, and restrictions on the power of representatives. Pay the statutory filing fee by secure electronic payment. The Registraire issues a Numéro d'entreprise du Québec (NEQ) and a certified attestation upon registration.
required_dossiers: Duly executed Declaration of Registration for a limited partnership
Name reservation or NUANS report reference number
Consent of the general partner with certified signature
Authorized person or filing agent's power of attorney (if applicable)
Payment confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registraire issues a notice of failure or query under s. 10 of the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, the declarant shall correct the deficiencies and file a rectifying declaration within 30 days; refusal may be appealed to the director of the Registraire and subsequently to the Cour du Québec.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registration for Federal and Provincial Tax Accounts
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Business Registration Online; Revenu Québec integrated business registration through the Registraire des entreprises
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After issuance of the NEQ, request the federal Business Number (BN), GST/HST account under Division V of the Excise Tax Act, and the Québec sales tax (QST) account under the Act respecting the Québec sales tax. Register for payroll source deductions (income tax, QPIP, QPP, EI) if the partnership will employ individuals. The partnership must generally file annual information returns; each period the partnership status must be declared.
required_dossiers: NEQ and attestation of registration
General partner's business and address details
Projected revenues to determine GST/QST filing frequency
Payroll information and expected staff count
Bank account authorization for tax direct debits (optional)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Delayed or refused accounts shall be remedied by submitting amended business particulars online or through CRA/Revenu Québec business phone services; late registrations can be backdated on request, and eligible taxpayers may apply for voluntary disclosure relief to reduce penalties.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Registration Publication, Certified Records and Amendment Declarations
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After the registration becomes effective, verify that the register contains all mandatory particulars (CCQ art. 2243), namely the name of the partnership, its head office, the general partner, the name and address of each limited partner, and the restrictions on the power of authorized representatives. Obtain a certified copy for banking and contracting. File an amending declaration within 30 days after any change of these particulars and file the annual update declaration each year before the service deadline.
required_dossiers: Certified copy of the declaration of registration
Confirmation of head office address
Copy of any restriction of powers or delegation document to be published
Annual update declaration reminder
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If inaccurate particulars are published, file a rectifying declaration; the registrar may also order a correction on its own motion. A person suffering prejudice may apply to the court for rectification under art. 37 of the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Municipal, Occupational Health and Fire Safety Compliance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Municipalité or Arrondissement (occupancy permit); Commission des normes, de l'équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST); Régie du bâtiment du Québec (RBQ)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: For the head office leased premises in Québec, obtain the landlord's consent and, where required by municipal by-law, a commercial occupancy permit (certificat d'occupation). Register with CNESST as an employer immediately upon hiring staff. Confirm landlord fire safety certificates and compliance with the Québec Safety Code; for software-only office use, no structural load inspection is required.
required_dossiers: Lease or registered office consent letter
Municipal commercial occupancy application and fee
CNESST employer registration form (after first employee)
Fire safety certificate or attestation from the building owner
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If municipal occupancy is refused, appeal the refusal to the municipal council or the administrative review body; for CNESST, contest any assessment by filing a notice of objection within the statutory period. Fire safety deficiencies are cured by the landlord's corrective action and issuance of an attestation.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable — no mandatory industrial licensing authority for a pure SaaS software activity under ISIC 6201. Where physical office premises are used, the Régie du bâtiment du Québec (RBQ) supervises building safety and the competent municipal authority issues the commercial occupancy permit.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No operating or manufacturing license is required for the PropTech real-estate SaaS platform; the only physical authorization applicable is the optional municipal commercial occupancy permit for the registered office (permis ou certificat d'occupation commerciale).

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Ministère de l'Environnement, de la Lutte contre les changements climatiques, de la Faune et des Parcs (MELCCFP), Direction de l'analyse des projets, Québec
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — A mandatory environmental impact assessment is not required for software-only operations; the activity falls outside the thresholds of the Regulation respecting environmental impact assessment and review (CQLR c. Q-2, r. 23) as it does not involve an industrial undertaking, construction or land alteration.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No industrial wastewater, VOC or exhaust emission thresholds apply. Office tenants must comply with municipal sewer use and recycling by-laws; waste electronics and IT equipment are governed by the Regulation respecting the recovery and reclamation of products by enterprises (CQLR c. Q-2, r. 40.1), requiring end-of-life electronics to be remitted to an accredited reclamation program.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety certification of the leased office premises pursuant to the Building Act (CQLR c. B-1.1) and the Québec Safety Code; workplace health and safety registration with the CNESST as an employer; electrical installation and emergency exit compliance confirmed by the landlord; occupancy permit issued by the municipality or arrondissement; no structural load inspection is required for standard office occupancy.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — federal income tax and GST/HST administration; portal: https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html. In Québec, Revenu Québec (RQ) administers the QST and provincial tax system; portal: https://www.revenuquebec.ca/en/. The Registraire des entreprises du Québec (https://www.registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca) issues the provincial NEQ.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Register the limited partnership with the Registraire des entreprises du Québec to obtain the NEQ (Quebec enterprise number). Step 2: Apply to the CRA for a federal Business Number (BN) using Business Registration Online (BRO) or Form RC1; request a GST/HST account (for the LP's taxable supplies) and a T5013/Partnership Information Return account. Step 3: Register for QST with Revenu Québec using Form LM-1 or the clicSÉCU Affaires online service, referencing the NEQ; RQ issues a separate QST account number. Non-resident partners may file via an authorized representative (CRA Form RC59 / RQ authorization mandate) and are allocated income through the partnership's T5013/TP-600 information returns; the LP itself remains transparent and is not a taxpayer.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible — a Québec LP is fiscally transparent under ITA s. 96 and the Québec Taxation Act: no entity-level tax; each partner includes its allocable share computed as if the partnership's activities were carried on by the partner directly. Non-resident partners remain taxable in Canada on Canadian-source partnership income (Part I) and may be subject to Part XIII withholding on certain passive allocations.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not provide a US-style check-the-box election. The transparent LP treatment is the default and is modified only via narrow statutory elections: (i) ITA s. 96(3) (with the parallel Québec provision) permits a partnership, on a joint prescribed-form election by all partners, to be deemed a corporation for limited income-tax purposes in specified cross-border contexts; (ii) a partnership may elect its fiscal period for tax purposes under ITA s. 249.1 and the Québec equivalent (December 31 remains the statutory default for most LPs); (iii) no hybrid-mismatch 'curative election' is available — Canada's anti-hybrid/EIFEL rules (ITA ss. 18.2/18.3 and related provisions) automatically disallow deductions for hybrid mismatch amounts; CRA administrative entity-classification guidance (Income Tax Folio S4-F3-C1) only recognizes foreign check-the-box outcomes for previously 'orphan' hybrid entities and cannot convert a domestic Québec LP into an opaque corporation for Canadian tax.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Federal GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) imposed under the Excise Tax Act, administered in Québec by Revenu Québec, combined with the Québec Sales Tax (QST) imposed under the Québec Sales Tax Act; standard combined rate on taxable B2B/B2C SaaS supplies in Québec is GST 5% + QST 9.5% = 14.5%.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 — the GST/HST and QST 'small supplier' threshold. Registration is mandatory when the LP's worldwide taxable supplies (other than zero-rated supplies) exceed CAD 30,000 in a single calendar quarter or in the four consecutive calendar quarters, measured equivalently for GST/HST (ETA s. 148) and QST (Québec Sales Tax Act); exports of SaaS services to non-residents that qualify as zero-rated are excluded from the threshold computation.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada and Québec do not currently mandate CTC (continuous transaction control) real-time clearance, digital fiscal stamps, or government pre-approval of invoices. Invoices must contain the prescribed GST/HST particulars and be issued for all taxable supplies. However, Revenu Québec has announced a phased mandatory e-invoicing and e-reporting regime for Québec taxable suppliers (pursuant to its 2023–2027 digitalization plan), commencing with large enterprises in the 2026–2027 window and extending to smaller businesses such as the subject LP in subsequent phases (target full-scope application before 2031); in-scope taxpayers must transmit structured e-invoices (e.g., PEPPOL/UBL format) through certified service providers and provide RQ with electronic sales reporting. For visibility at present, the LP must keep its SaaS billing records (Stripe Billing, ACH) in an auditable electronic format and file GST/HST/QST returns electronically.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating (0% GST/HST and QST) is available for a supply of a 'specified service' — including SaaS/software services — made to a non-resident recipient, provided the service is not in respect of real property situated in Canada and not in respect of tangible personal property situated in Canada, and provided the recipient is outside Canada at the time the service is rendered (ETA Schedule VI Part V s. 7; mirror QST rule). For the PropTech/real-estate platform, the supply must be characterized as a software/platform service delivered electronically to non-resident clients; if the platform also manages, markets, or screens Canadian real-property portfolios (i.e., the supply relates to Quebec real property), the zero-rating is unavailable and the full supply is taxable at 14.5%. Intermediary B2B supplies to non-resident resellers may also qualify if the reseller's onward supply is to other non-residents and the Canadian supplier has no knowledge of supply to Canada.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: GST/HST and QST export invoice issued electronically showing 'Export / Zero-Rated (0%)' and the non-resident recipient's billing address outside Canada
Signed SaaS Master Subscription Agreement / order form identifying the non-resident client, jurisdiction of use, and delivery method (no Canadian land nexus)
Non-resident status evidence (foreign business registration extract or tax-residence certificate, plus the client's declaration that it is not resident in Canada)
Delivery and usage records (server/API access logs, IP geolocation evidence, customer onboarding records) demonstrating actual offshore receipt of the SaaS
Payment/consideration records (Stripe Billing payout statements, ACH/SWIFT receipts) tracing consideration from the non-resident payer

Where tangible hardware (e.g., IoT sensors for property management) is exported: CBSA export documentation (B13A / eManifest export reporting), bill of lading or airway waybill, and proof of export within a reasonable time
If applicable, a Form GST189 or CRA-issued non-resident registration proof for the purchaser (only for goods consigned to Canada for export)

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), with the foreign exchange policy function formally assigned to the Minister of Finance and administered through the Bank of Canada; prudential supervision of federally regulated banks is performed by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI). Canada does not operate a centralized foreign-exchange control administration or exchange-control licensing bureau.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is freely convertible on both capital and current accounts. Canada accepts IMF Article VIII status, meaning there are no exchange-control restrictions on payments or transfers for current international transactions, no prior approval for profit remittances, and no restriction on holding foreign currency in Canada or abroad. Capital account flows, including non-resident limited partner capital contributions, partnership distributions, and repatriation of invested funds, are generally unrestricted; the only material hurdles are standard AML/KYC requirements, FINTRAC electronic funds transfer reports for transactions equal to or above CAD 10,000, sanctions screening under the United Nations Act and the Special Economic Measures Act, Investment Canada Act review for large or national-security-sensitive acquisitions, and ordinary Canadian and Quebec income tax compliance including any applicable treaty-based withholding characterization. For a Quebec PropTech SaaS limited partnership, profit remittance presents no FX-control blockage and is constrained only by tax reporting, account documentation, and banking compliance.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Not applicable. Canada imposes no statutory export-proceeds surrender regime, no mandatory conversion timeline, and no minimum conversion ratio for export receipts. Exporters may lawfully retain foreign currency in Canadian or offshore accounts and convert to CAD at commercial market rates whenever commercially desired. Documentary compliance is nonetheless required: retain executed export or SaaS subscription contracts and payment records for CRA purposes, comply with CBSA export declaration requirements where goods are exported, and ensure the receiving bank files any required FINTRAC EFT report when an incoming wire equals or exceeds CAD 10,000. There is no central-bank directive requiring repatriation of export proceeds within a fixed number of days.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: National Bank of Canada / Banque Nationale du Canada

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada / RBC Royal Bank

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: The Bank of Nova Scotia / Scotiabank
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account and FX Treasury Account for USD/CAD liquidity management

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Medium as a payment-processing auxiliary but Low as a primary treasury relationship. An offshore digital EMI cannot act as a bank in Canada unless authorized under the Bank Act; for payment services it must be registered as a money services business with FINTRAC and, if operating in Quebec, must hold a money-services-business permit issued by the Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF). A non-resident EMI is also subject to the federal Retail Payment Activities Act and may be required to register with the Bank of Canada once the registration phase is fully in force. The compliant architecture is to maintain the principal Escrow and Operating Accounts at a Tier 1 Canadian Schedule I bank and use a licensed EMI or PSP solely as a supplementary disbursement rail, with daily zero-balance sweeps back to the Canadian bank. Investment of partner capital or dividend distribution must not be warehoused through an unregulated offshore EMI.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Canadian bank policy is not uniform. In practice, for a newly formed Quebec LP with non-resident limited partners, at least one authorized signatory, normally the managing general partner or a Quebec-resident compliance officer, will be required to attend an in-person onboarding interview at the bank's commercial office in Quebec, typically Montreal. Remote opening is possible for the remaining signatories and for non-resident limited partners only if identity documents are notarized or apostilled, the entity's beneficial ownership chain is fully transparent, the bank has no adverse sanctions or risk findings, and the partnership provides current Registry of Quebec Enterprises (Registraire des entreprises) evidence and source-of-funds documentation. A Canadian resident general partner or authorized officer should appear physically to maximize onboarding viability.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident limited partners or authorized signatories domiciled in high-risk, sanctioned, or non-FATF-compliant jurisdictions.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide the complete beneficial ownership schedule with notarized passports for every partner holding 10% or more, current Registraire des entreprises du Québec attestation, executed partnership agreement, home-bank professional reference, source-of-wealth evidence such as three years of personal tax returns or financial statements, and a Quebec legal opinion confirming that the LP is not an offshore issuer and that all contributions are sourced from lawful commercial activity.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-volume, low-ticket SaaS merchant transactions without transparent linkage to the real-estate PropTech service being provided.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Deliver the full commercial product pack: executed master subscription agreements, current terms of use and privacy policy, client onboarding/KYC summaries, sample invoices, refund and chargeback history, monthly transaction reports from Stripe Billing and ACH Direct settlement, a SOC 2 Type II report, PCI DSS attestation of compliance, and an audit trail reconciling merchant settlement amounts to contracted recurring SaaS fees for the real-estate screening and property management platform.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Use of an offshore EMI or third-party payment processor as a deposit or treasury node, giving rise to commingling or unauthorized deposit-taking concerns.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Submit the FINTRAC registration of the processor or EMI, Quebec money-services-business licence where applicable, the contractual payment facilitation agreement, a no-deposit-taking legal opinion, a daily-zero-balance sweep mandate to the primary Canadian bank, monthly independent reconciliation reports, and a written undertaking that no partner capital or distribution proceeds will be held with the unregulated processor beyond the minimum operating settlement period.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inconsistencies between the Quebec registry information, beneficial ownership declarations, and source of funds for a non-resident partner, triggering enhanced due diligence.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide a reconciliation letter from a Quebec licensed public accountant or notary, updated registre extract, proof of residential or business address for each partner dated within 90 days, tax identification number or equivalent for every beneficial owner, independent PEP and sanctions screening reports, and a source-of-funds memorandum supported by bank statements and asset-transaction records.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Non-resident limited partner capital injections should be routed as a single clean wire through SWIFT MT103 or the equivalent ISO 20022 pacs.008 message to the Capital Escrow Account held at the selected Schedule I Canadian bank. The remittance information field must clearly state: CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION, followed by the exact legal name of the Quebec LP and the partner reference. Canada imposes no national mandatory purpose-code taxonomy for cross-border wires, so the bank's portal should be completed with the reason for payment categorized as capital investment or treasury contribution rather than trade invoice; where an ISO ExternalPurposeCode is mandatory in the correspondent bank system, use the bank-accepted commercial payment or capital transfer code displayed by the sending bank's treasury portal. The verification package must include the executed limited partnership subscription agreement, capital call notice, source-of-funds documentation for each contributing partner, tax identification data, and a FINTRAC record where the wire is equal to or exceeds CAD 10,000. Contributions above CAD 100,000 will normally trigger enhanced due diligence and may require the partner's audited financials or constitutional documents. Payments must never be fragmented to avoid FINTRAC reporting thresholds.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound disbursements should be executed through the primary bank using the following clearing hierarchy: (i) SWIFT MT103 / ISO 20022 pacs.008 for international vendor payments, non-resident partner distributions, and cross-border service fees, with a meaningful purpose narrative in the remittance field; (ii) Fedwire or CHIPS via the bank's U.S. correspondent for high-value USD wires; (iii) NACHA ACH via the bank's U.S. clearing account for USD ACH Direct payouts to U.S.-based vendors and contractors; (iv) Payments Canada ACSS for domestic CAD direct debit and credit payments, and LVTS for high-value same-day CAD transfers; and (v) commercial letters of credit, issued by SWIFT MT700 or MT710, for hardware procurement or other equipment imports used in the PropTech solution, with confirmation from an overseas correspondent bank where supplier risk requires it. The Canadian LP should maintain both CAD and USD accounts at the primary bank to avoid duplicate FX conversion and should use a single clearing treasury node for all disbursements.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright deliverable USD/CAD forward contracts, typically up to 24 months, used to fix the CAD cost of known USD expenditures or to protect the CAD value of contracted USD subscription revenue.

FX swap or rollover transactions executed with the primary bank to convert temporary USD cash surpluses into CAD without creating an open-market position and while preserving the ability to reverse the conversion for the next USD vendor payout.
Cross-currency basis swap, receive USD and pay CAD, under ISDA/CSA documentation, for the notional amount of USD-denominated LP capital held in the treasury program.

Non-deliverable forward (NDF) permitted only where an invoiced settlement currency is not freely deliverable in the Canadian interbank market; subject to prior treasury committee approval, supported by an underlying commercial exposure, and never used for speculative positions.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Quebec Annual Declaration (Déclaration de mise à jour annuelle) to the Registraire des entreprises du Québec (REQ)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the anniversary date of initial registration; a different initial window may apply during the year of first registration.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of CAD 33 (approx. USD 25); persistent non-filing for three consecutive annual cycles can lead to administrative strike-off of the LP registration and personal liability exposure of the general partner.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T5013 Partnership Information Return (Summary and Supplementary Forms)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 6 months after the partnership fiscal year-end; for a calendar-year partnership, due on or before June 30 of the following year.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of CAD 25 per partner per day, subject to a minimum of CAD 100 and a maximum of CAD 2,500 per partner; continued non-filing may trigger CRA audit, reassessment of partner allocations, and additional penalties against the general partner or filing responsible party.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory independent audit is imposed by Quebec partnership law or the Quebec Enterprise Registration Act on a Limited Partnership. Audit obligations arise only if required by the Limited Partnership Agreement, a lender or investor, or if the partnership is a public reporting issuer under Canadian securities legislation.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Identifier - Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE) per the CPA Canada Handbook; IFRS is required if the entity becomes a publicly accountable enterprise. Books must support Canadian Income Tax Act reporting of partnership income, losses, allocations, contributions, and distributions.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: In Quebec, the annual declaration requires confirmation of each individual who is a controller of the enterprise, including the general partner and any party with de jure or de facto control. Transfers of limited partnership units are not separately declared to the REQ except where the identity of a controlling individual changes; however, the LP's internal Register of Partners must be updated for every transfer, contribution, or distribution. Any change in registered particulars (including a change of general partner or registered address) must be reported to the REQ by way of a notice of modification generally within 30 days of the event.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Limited Partners and Capital Contributions
Register of General Partner Resolutions / Decision Log
Minute Book containing LP agreement amendments and partner consent records

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 95 - 250 per year for a Quebec registered office and corporate agent services
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 4,000 - 8,500 per year for a small to mid-size PropTech/real-estate SaaS limited partnership, only if contractually or lender-required

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.5% combined federal and Quebec statutory corporate income tax rate for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) earning active business income eligible for the federal small business deduction, before provincial abatement adjustments; general federal rate 15%, Quebec rate 11.5%, resulting in 26.5% for non-CCPC or general income; active business income under the CCPC small business limit is subject to a reduced combined rate of approximately 12.2% (federal 9% effective after abatement plus Quebec 3.2% small business deduction rate), with the federal small business limit of CAD 500,000 and Quebec small business limit of CAD 500,000, subject to phase-out rules.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Federal small business deduction (SBD): 9% federal rate on first CAD 500,000 of active business income, phased out when taxable capital exceeds CAD 10 million and when adjusted aggregate investment income exceeds CAD 50,000; Quebec small business deduction: reduces Quebec rate to 3.2% on first CAD 500,000 of active business income, phased out at taxable capital between CAD 15 million and CAD 35 million; Quebec refundable tax credit for investment and innovation (C3i) up to 30% on eligible expenditures; Quebec interactive digital media tax credit up to 30% on eligible labour expenditures; SR&ED federal and Quebec refundable investment tax credits; Quebec film or multimedia production tax credits; federal and Quebec accelerated capital cost allowance (CCA) for software and cloud infrastructure (Class 12, Class 50, and Class 29 for manufacturing or processing equipment); Quebec tax credit for on-the-job training; federal and Quebec foreign tax credits for foreign-source income; no provincial capital tax in Quebec for corporations; Quebec payroll tax exemption for small businesses where total payroll below CAD 7,200,000.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed via the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) electronic filing system (GST/HST and corporate e-filing portal, CRA My Business Account, or approved third-party EDI software) for federal purposes; Quebec corporation income tax return (form CO-17, Rapport d'impôt sur le revenu des sociétés) filed via Revenu Québec's electronically secure portal (clicsour / mon dossier d'entreprise).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Filing deadline is six months after the corporation's fiscal year-end; e.g., a December 31 fiscal year-end requires filing by June 30 of the following calendar year; balance of tax payable is due two months after the fiscal year-end for Canadian-controlled private corporations claiming the small business deduction, or three months after fiscal year-end for non-CCPCs and for CCPCs without SBD claims, except where a corporation is a Canadian-controlled private corporation with taxable income exceeding CAD 500,000 or with a prior-year association, the payment due date reverts to the two-month rule; Quebec CO-17 filing due date aligns with the same six-month rule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Box 1 / Line 1a (T2) and Quebec CO-17 Line 1
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Identification of the taxpayer: legal name, Business Number (BN) / Quebec Enterprise Number (NEQ), registered office address, jurisdiction of formation, fiscal year-end date, and indication of limited partnership status for the entity; note that a Canadian resident limited partnership is a flow-through entity for income tax purposes, but the T2 return is filed by the corporate general partner for the partnership's Canadian-source income calculation or the partnership files a prescribed information return (T5013 Summary and T5013 Supplementary forms for each partner) to report each partner's share of income, losses, and resource allowances.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident corporate partner (or limited partner) of the Quebec limited partnership, the T5013 forms and CO-17-related schedules must identify the non-resident partner's name, address, country of residence, tax identification number in the country of residence, percentage of partnership interests, and share of each category of Canadian-source partnership income or loss; the corporate general partner resident in Canada remits and files on behalf of the partnership; non-resident partners without a permanent establishment in Canada but deriving Canadian-source income through a partnership that carries on business in Canada or that owns Canadian real estate or Canadian resource property may be liable for Part XIV non-resident tax under section 212 of the Income Tax Act, including withholding on any distribution characterized as a dividend, interest, royalty, or rental payment, and must generally file a T2 return or a T1 return if an individual, or a prescribed NR6 undertaking if the non-resident partner elects to file a Canadian return to claim treaty relief; the non-resident partner should also obtain a Canadian BN and complete Form RC416 (Application for a Canadian Business Number) if not already registered.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Fiscal period and residency status: declaration of the date the corporation or partnership became resident in Canada, whether the entity is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), a public corporation, or a non-resident owned corporation, and whether the corporation has a permanent establishment in Quebec; for a limited partnership, the partnership's residence is generally determined by the residency of its controlling general partner, but the partnership is not itself a taxpayer for income tax purposes; instead each partner reports its allocable share of income or loss on its own return, and the T5013 Summary describes the allocation formula.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident partners must indicate their treaty residency status and claim withholding tax relief by submitting a completed NR301 (Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits Under a Tax Convention) for withholding at source, or by filing a prescribed tax return (T2 or T1159) to report Canadian-source income; for partnership allocations, the non-resident partner's share of Canadian-source business income is taxable on a net basis under Part I if the partnership carries on business in Canada through a permanent establishment, or under Part XIII withholding rules for passive income such as rents or royalties when no permanent establishment exists.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Line 3 / Schedule 1, and Quebec CO-17 Line 3 and Schedule A
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculation of taxable income: total revenues from cloud subscription services and real estate property management SaaS fees, cost of sales, general and administrative expenses, depreciation and amortization, Canadian and foreign source income, capital gains and allowable business investment losses, partnership income or loss allocations, and other deductions; specifically for a PropTech SaaS platform, revenue recognition under the accrual method follows the contractual subscription period, and unredeemed deferred revenue must be tracked separately from the partnership's distributable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident partners' shares of taxable income are computed under the same provisions, but with treaty restrictions: a non-resident partner's business income from the Quebec partnership is only taxable in Canada if attributable to a permanent establishment in Canada; for software-as-a-service payments, income characterization as business profits versus royalties is critical, and the Canada-US treaty or Canada-Jurisdiction treaty will generally allocate business profits only to a permanent establishment, while royalty income may be subject to 25% Canadian withholding subject to treaty reduction; transfer pricing adjustments may reallocate profits under section 247 of the Income Tax Act.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Line 4 / Schedule 3, Quebec CO-17 Line 4
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital cost allowance (depreciation) and cumulative eligible capital deductions: software development costs capitalized under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles may be deductible at accelerated rates; Class 12 (100% for computer software of a prescribed type), Class 50 (55% straight-line declining balance for general-purpose computer hardware and systems software), Class 52 (100% for acquired software in certain periods), and Class 43.1/43.2 for clean energy equipment; cloud infrastructure expenditures may be treated as current expenses, while in-house SaaS platform development costs may be claimed under SR&ED investment tax credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident partners cannot directly claim CCA unless they themselves carry on business in Canada; the partnership computes CCA at the partnership level and allocates the net income or loss to partners; a non-resident partner's distributable share from the partnership is subject to the same permanent establishment threshold; capital gains from dispositions of Canadian real estate by a partnership may trigger a non-resident vendor notification and withholding obligation under section 116 of the Income Tax Act, requiring a clearance certificate.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Line 5 / Schedule 5 and Parts I-IV, Quebec CO-17 Line 5 and related schedules
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provincial allocation of taxable income among jurisdictions: for a limited partnership carrying on business in Quebec and possibly other Canadian provinces, the income is allocated among permanent establishments using gross revenue and salary and wages factors under the Income Tax Regulations and Quebec Taxation Act rules; the PropTech SaaS company will allocate revenue based on the location of servers, sales personnel, and management, with Quebec effectively using a 50/50 formula between gross revenues and salaries and wages attributable to each permanent establishment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident partners' treaty benefits are applied independently of provincial allocation; where a non-resident partner does not have a permanent establishment in Quebec but the partnership does, Quebec may still tax the partner's share of income attributable to the Quebec permanent establishment because under Canadian federal-provincial allocation the non-resident is deemed to have a permanent establishment in Quebec through the partnership.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Line 6 / Quebec CO-17 Line 2 (Quebec equivalent) and Schedule C
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign tax credit calculation: credit for foreign income taxes paid on foreign-source income included in the partnership's income allocation; for a SaaS business with customers in the US via ACH Direct, any US federal or state income taxes paid on profits attributable to a US permanent establishment (e.g., a US office or dependent agent) are creditable against Canadian and Quebec income taxes on that same income; excess foreign tax credits cannot exceed the Canadian tax otherwise payable on that foreign-source income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident partner's foreign-source income generally only enters the Canadian computation if the partner is a Canadian resident for tax purposes; foreign tax credits are not available to non-resident partners unless they are otherwise taxable in Canada on that income under a treaty provision that preserves tax credit.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Line 7 / Schedules 7 and 8, Quebec CO-17 Line 106
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Small business deduction computation: eligibility of the corporate general partner's active business income from the partnership for the federal small business deduction and Quebec deduction; active business income includes income from the SaaS platform operations provided the income is not specified investment business income (e.g., income from property that is not active business), and does not exceed the CAD 500,000 business limit; associated CCPC rules require aggregation with associated corporations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident partners are not entitled to the small business deduction because they are not Canadian-controlled private corporations; the deduction remains available to the Canadian-resident corporate general partner but must be allocated based on the general partner's share of active business income; a non-resident partner's share of partnership income is not eligible for the SBD and any attempted transfer of the deduction to a non-resident partner is a fatal misrepresentation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Schedule 6 / Quebec CO-17 Schedule F
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Dividend / distribution tracking: even though an LP is generally flow-through in Quebec and federal, the partnership must record each partner's capital account, draws, and distributions; distributions of retained earnings that have not been taxed at the partnership level are not deductible at the partnership level and are simply a return of capital or taxable distributions to partners; the corporate general partner must also compute refundable dividend tax on hand and eligible/non-eligible dividend designations for any dividends it pays to shareholders.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: When a non-resident partner receives a distribution of partnership income that is a payment of a dividend, royalty, rent, or interest from the partnership, the partnership (or resident payor) must withhold non-resident withholding tax at the statutory rate of 25%, subject to treaty reduction; for a distribution of pure partnership business income, no withholding applies if the non-resident partner has filed an NR301 and the income is attributable to a Canadian permanent establishment; otherwise withholding under Part XIII may be exigible on deemed dividends or on management fees.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 — Schedule 15 / Quebec CO-17 Schedule G
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Related party and transfer pricing disclosure: identification of all cross-border transactions with non-arm's length persons, including software licensing fees paid to a foreign parent, royalties received from US customers, management fees paid to a non-resident service provider, and loans to foreign shareholders; the Canadian transfer pricing documentation form (Form T106, Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents) must disclose each transaction and the arm's length methodology applied.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The non-resident shareholder or related party must ensure the Quebec LP's cross-border payments are priced at arm's length; failure to do so triggers penalties under subsection 247(3) of the Income Tax Act equal to 10% of the net transfer pricing adjustment, plus interest, and may be subject to a gross negligence penalty of 50% of the adjustment where misrepresentation is attributable to culpable conduct.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Failure to file a T2 return on time: penalty equal to 5% of the unpaid balance of tax, plus 1% for each complete month the return is late, up to a maximum of 12 months, for Canada; a further penalty of 10% of the tax due may apply where a late-filing penalty was issued in the prior three years; failure to file the Quebec CO-17 return: penalty equal to 5% of the tax due, plus 1% per month of delinquency up to a maximum of 12 months, up to a maximum penalty of CAD 10,000 for a corporation; failure to file the T5013 partnership information return: penalty of CAD 25 per unregistered partner per slip (maximum CAD 2,500), or CAD 100 per partner per slip (maximum CAD 7,500) plus a penalty equal to CAD 24 per missed partner per day for partnerships with more than 10 partners, capped at CAD 1,000 for the first 90 days and an additional CAD 1,000 thereafter; late or omitted information in Form T106: penalty of CAD 100 per month per person (maximum CAD 2,500 for reasonable failure), increased to CAD 1,000 per month (maximum CAD 25,000) for a participating partner's failure to file for the purpose of making a transfer pricing adjustment; interest on unpaid tax accrued daily at the prescribed rate (currently 9% for corporations for the period of July 1, 2025, to September 30, 2025, compounded daily); Quebec late-filing penalty applies analogously plus a daily interest rate on balance due; a 10% gross negligence penalty under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act applies to false statements, and similarly under section 1019 of the Quebec Taxation Act; directors may be liable for amounts withheld but not remitted under section 227.1 of the Income Tax Act and section 325 of the Quebec Taxation Act.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% statutory withholding on dividends paid or credited by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident beneficial owner, under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act, and 25% under Quebec's equivalent withholding provisions (Quebec Taxation Act); for a limited partnership, withholding is not triggered by the mere distribution of the partner's tax-paid earnings except where the distribution is characterized as a dividend from a corporation deemed to be resident in Canada or where the partnership makes a payment of interest, rent, royalties, or management fees to a non-resident partner; the higher statutory rate applies unless a tax treaty reduces it.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke a reduced dividend withholding tax rate under a Canada tax treaty, the non-resident beneficial owner must: (1) obtain a certificate of residence (Form NR301 for Canada, or Form 6166 from the US IRS, or equivalent from the treaty partner's tax authority) evidencing tax residence in the treaty jurisdiction; (2) submit a completed Form NR301 (Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits Under a Tax Convention) to the Canadian payor or partnership before payment; (3) provide Form NR302 or Form NR303 as applicable to claim treaty-reduced rates on dividends or royalties; (4) for US persons, certify eligibility under the Canada-US Tax Convention's limitation on benefits (LOB) article; (5) ensure the beneficial owner is the actual recipient and not an agent, nominee, or conduit; (6) file an NR4 information return with the CRA to report the gross amount and the reduced rate applied; the CRA will require the foreign tax authority to have issued a TRC reflecting the applicable article; for Quebec purposes, Revenu Québec requires a separate certificate of residence and the filing of the Quebec form RL-016 or similar election; where the partnership itself is a flow-through entity, the transparent status must be proven to obtain treaty benefits for the partners; the protocol must also be applied before the payment or within an acceptable retroactive timeline, generally the date of filing of the NR4 and the date of the TRC; failure to complete the protocol subjects the non-resident recipient to the statutory 25% rate and potential recapture penalties.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Canadian withholding tax rate on royalties for the use of intellectual property, patents, trademarks, know-how, software copyright, or similar property paid to a non-resident: 25% under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act; interest payments to a non-arm's length non-resident creditor exceeding prescribed thresholds: 25% statutory rate, subject to exceptions for arm's length interest paid to a resident of a treaty country, interest paid on certain foreign-denominated or exempt obligations, and interest paid to a permanent establishment; under the Canada-US tax treaty, royalties generally are subject to 0% US withholding (for US recipients) or 10% for certain industrial royalties, whereas interest is generally exempt from Canadian withholding when the recipient is a US resident under Article XI (0% treaty rate for arm's length interest); for other treaty jurisdictions, royalty rates are typically 10% (e.g., Canada-France, Canada-Germany, Canada-Italy) and interest rates 10% to 15% (often 10% for France, 15% for Italy, 0% or 10% depending on the treaty); a Quebec limited partnership must also impose Quebec withholding tax at the provincial statutory rate of 15% on royalties and interest paid to non-residents unless a treaty abolishes or reduces the Quebec withholding; Quebec generally follows the treaty rates but requires a separate treaty certificate; software payments for cloud SaaS are often characterized as business profits rather than royalties under modern treaty practice if no IP alienation or transfer of know-how occurs, which can eliminate withholding altogether when no permanent establishment exists; characterization risk triggers the fatal withholding exposure if the payor fails to withhold on payments later recharacterized as royalties.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: For Canadian federal tax purposes, Transfer Pricing Master File (TPMF) and Local File (TPLF) documentation are required for taxation years beginning on or after July 1, 2020, where: (a) the aggregate fair market value of transactions with non-resident related parties exceeds CAD 1,000,000 for acquisitions, dispositions, or loans; (b) the total amount of intercompany services charged exceeds CAD 1,000,000; or (c) the entity has gross revenue over CAD 50,000,000; Master File must be produced within 3 months after the corporation's fiscal year-end and Local File within 6 months after the fiscal year-end; Quebec's provincial transfer pricing documentation threshold mirrors the federal requirements under the Taxation Act, and Revenu Québec may demand production of prescribed documentation (Form CO-552) when transactions with non-residents exceed CAD 1,000,000 per year; for this PropTech SaaS platform with a cross-border US revenue stream, mandatory Local File and Master File thresholds are triggered when gross royalty-like payments, intercompany management fees, technology license fees, or any related-party loans from non-residents exceed CAD 1,000,000; the Canadian documentation must include the transactional business strategy, contractual terms, economic analysis, and benchmark comparability study.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Under Canada's general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) in section 245 of the Income Tax Act, a transaction must have a bona fide purpose, economic substance, and cannot be structured solely to avoid taxes; although Quebec does not have standalone Economic Substance Regulations modelled on the UAE or Cayman ESR, the federal income tax system and Revenu Québec's anti-avoidance provisions (Quebec Taxation Act sections 1074.1 to 1074.3) apply an economic substance doctrine requiring that the entity carry on real business activity, employ staff, incur operating expenses, assume economic risk, and exercise real decision-making functions (people functions) in Canada; a Quebec limited partnership used for a PropTech SaaS platform must demonstrate that the commercial substance, intellectual property ownership, and profit attribution align with the actual performance of significant people functions (i.e., product development, sales, customer support, and management) in Quebec; the CRA's transfer pricing rules under section 247 and the OECD's profit attribution principles in the Authorised OECD Approach (AOA) apply to attribute profits to a permanent establishment, requiring capital and risk allocation consistent with decision-making; a purely passive limited partnership holding IP in Quebec with its developers and managers located elsewhere or in a low-tax jurisdiction will be challenged as a sham or as a conduit, with the result that profits are reattributed to the jurisdiction of value creation; there is no regime of formal 'ESR filings' in Canada, but the CRA's Form T106 and Schedule 91 disclose economic substance indicators, and failure to maintain substance triggers GAAR reassessment, 10% transfer pricing penalty under subsection 247(3), gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2), and possible criminal liability under subsection 239(1).

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately omitting US-sourced SaaS subscription revenue from the partnership's T5013 allocations, underreporting gross income, claiming personal expenses as business expenses, destruction of accounting records, or making false statements in the T2 or CO-17 filings; knowingly issuing false invoices to a non-resident related patent-holding company to strip profits out of Canada; failing to file the T5013 partnership information return.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under subsection 239(1) of the Income Tax Act and section 1027 of the Quebec Taxation Act, tax evasion is an indictable offence subject to imprisonment for up to 5 years, fines of up to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded, or both; the CRA may impose a civil penalty under subsection 163(2) equal to 50% of the understated tax (gross negligence penalty), plus interest and arrears; Quebec imposes an equivalent gross negligence penalty of 50% on the federal penalty plus a Quebec-specific penalty of 50%; the court may order restitution, forfeiture, and costs; repeated evasion triggers escalated fines not exceeding 200% of the tax evaded under both federal and provincial statutes.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the Canadian corporate general partner may have their personal liability pierced under subsection 227.1(1) of the Income Tax Act and section 325 of the Quebec Taxation Act for failure to withhold or remit Part XIII withholding tax, employee source deductions, or GST/HST/QST amounts; directors may be personally liable for divided penalties and the Crown's right of recovery under section 227.1 may be enforced even if the corporation is dissolved; where tax evasion is committed with fraudulent intent, the court may impose a travel ban, a criminal conviction creating a criminal record affecting US ESTA and Canadian immigration status, seizure of personal assets via a civil fraud judgment, and imprisonment of up to 5 years; the CRA's Voluntary Disclosure Program may shield taxpayers only before a formal investigation or compliance enforcement notice is issued.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Penalty and Thin Capitalization
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Entering into non-arm's length transactions with a non-resident related party without contemporaneous documentation, such as overpaying a Bermuda or Cayman parent for software licences, charging artificially high royalty rates on IP licensed into Canada to shift profits, or structuring the partnership with excessive shareholder debt in a non-resident's hands exceeding the prescribed debt-to-equity ratio of 1.5:1 (for debts owing to specified non-resident shareholders or partnerships), or making cross-border loans at non-arm's length interest above the prescribed rate; failing to prepare and retain the T106 return and master/local file.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under subsection 247(3) of the Income Tax Act, a penalty of 10% of the net transfer pricing adjustment, with a minimum penalty of CAD 5,000 for failure to make or to file complete and accurate T106 information, and CAD 2,500 additional penalties for repeated failure; in addition, the denial of interest deductions on excessive debt under thin capitalization rules (subsection 18(4) and section 212(1)(b)) subjects the excessive amounts to a 25% withholding tax on deemed interest, and the CRA may impose a gross negligence penalty of 50% of the reassessed tax under subsection 163(2); Revenu Québec applies equivalent penalties and adjustments under sections 441.34 and 1018.1 of the Quebec Taxation Act, including a 10% penalty on the Quebec transfer pricing adjustment and a 50% penalty for false statements.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the general partner may be personally liable under section 247(5) of the Income Tax Act where the penalty arises from the directors' direction or consent, or where the corporation fails to withhold Part XIII tax on the excess debt interest; the doctrine of piercing the corporate veil applies under Quebec civil law (Civil Code of Quebec, articles 317 and 316) where the corporation is a mere agent or alter ego, making the directors personally responsible for the mischaracterized payments; the CRA may issue a director liability assessment under subsection 227.1(2) requiring immediate payment of unremitted withholding tax, interest, and penalties; personal liability can extend to the non-resident partner if it directs the management of the partnership and is de facto controlling the general partner, and can also be enforced through a Fraude de la loi action under civil law, leading to receivership over personal assets and prohibition on leaving Canada.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Sham and GAAR Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Creating the Quebec limited partnership or a non-resident holding vehicle without real employees, offices, bank accounts, or operational substance while routing US SaaS subscription payments through the entity solely to claim the Canada-US treaty benefits or to defer Canadian taxation; entering into circular or self-cancelling transactions designed to convert active SaaS business income into capital gains or to shift income to a tax haven; failing to demonstrate profit attribution with actual management decisions in Canada; using the partnership with the intent to circumvent the general 25% non-resident withholding on a deemed dividend or royalty.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA will invoke the general anti-avoidance rule (section 245) to deny the tax benefit and recharacterize the transaction, and may impose a penalty of 50% of the tax avoided under subsection 163(2) if the misrepresentation is attributable to culpable conduct; Revenu Québec invokes its equivalent GAAR (section 1074.1 of the Taxation Act) to deny the benefit and imposes penalties up to 50% of the Quebec tax avoided; a shell company may be refused treaty benefits under the principal purpose test (PPT) in the Canada-US multilateral instrument or the LOB clause in the Canada-US treaty; tax consequences include complete reassessment of all years within the normal reassessment period (three years, unaffected by fraud) and criminal sanctions under subsection 239(1) for misleading statements.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Under Quebec civil law, the corporate veil is pierced under articles 316–317 of the Civil Code of Quebec when the corporation or partnership is used to commit fraud, abuse of rights, or contravention of public order; directors are personally liable for the full amount of taxes, penalties, and interest, as well as for damages to the Crown; travel restrictions under s. 19.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act may apply while an appeal is pending, and an officer with a conviction for tax evasion faces a travel bar to Canada and the US (under the US Immigration and Nationality Act section 212(a)(2)(A)(i)(I) for crimes involving moral turpitude); officers and directors may also be jointly and severally liable under the OECD's new tax transparency rulings, and bank secrecy treatment does not protect the personal tax identity.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Proceeds of Crime
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the PropTech SaaS platform as a conduit for launder the proceeds of crime through Stripe_Billing or ACH_Direct payment rails by accepting payments from unrelated non-resident third parties without verifying beneficial ownership or by issuing fake real-estate rental screening invoices; failing to register with FINTRAC under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA) if the business provides money services or real estate brokerage, or repeatedly receiving large virtual currency or wire transfers; for a regular SaaS payment processor, low-risk AML status does not exempt the entity from maintaining a know-your-customer policy for high-risk US clients.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the PCMLTFA, failure to comply with registration, record-keeping, and reporting obligations can result in administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 500,000 for individuals and CAD 1,000,000 for entities per violation, and criminal penalties under the Criminal Code for laundering proceeds of crime carry imprisonment up to 10 years; Quebec's Act respecting the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing may impose fines and suspension of licences; if the payment rails are used for a prohibited predicate offense, the funds are subject to forfeiture; the Canada Revenue Agency can also impose a 50% civil penalty on the unreported income under subsection 163(2), and bank account freezing orders under the Criminal Code section 462.33.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers can be charged as parties to the offence under the Criminal Code for knowingly directing, authorizing, or acquiescing to the laundering or false reporting; the corporate veil is pierced under articles 316–317 of the Civil Code of Quebec, exposing personal assets; they are subject to imprisonment of up to 10 years for money laundering, 5 years for false accounting; they may face travel bans and civil asset forfeiture; FINTRAC compliance orders can be issued against individuals as designated officers without requiring a separate corporate shell; banking relationships are terminated, and directors become personally liable to banks for losses caused by the breach.
